overview: The Severians, or Siverianians, were East Slavic communities associated with the Desna and the upper Seim, Sula, Psel and Vorskla regions. This imported 700 to 800 outline omits substantial territory farther east. Bytytsia and Novotroitske, discussed below, lie beyond its eastern edge and provide regional comparisons. Archaeological traditions and chronicle names do not establish a single kingdom with surveyed borders.

periods.title: Communities of the river valleys
periods.summary: An eighth-century map interval, not the full lifetime of the Severian name.

sections.title: A large settlement on the Psel

items.text: At Bytytsia, east of this imported outline, a fortified settlement stood high above the Psel. Excavator Oleg Sukhobokov dates it from the middle of the eighth century to the turn of the ninth. Its area exceeded seven hectares, making it an unusually substantial site among the Volyntseve settlements associated with this region.

Excavation at Bytytsia uncovered more than sixty dwellings, around 250 metal objects and two hoards containing ornaments and tools. These discoveries bring domestic work and valued possessions into the story. They are totals from archaeological investigation, rather than a headcount of families living there on one particular day.

Sukhobokov interpreted Bytytsia’s contrasting material traditions as evidence of Slavic and Turkic inhabitants with different economic backgrounds. That proposed mixture helps explain why the site is discussed as a meeting place. Objects support an interpretation of cultural contact; they do not reveal each household’s spoken language.

sections.title: Pots, crops and the work of feeding people

items.text: Volyntseve pottery included both handmade vessels and locally produced wheel-made pottery. Sukhobokov stresses that handmade pots and bowls still formed the main part of the assemblage. A skilled new technique could coexist with familiar ways of making everyday containers.

The wheel-made vessels were distinctive enough in shape and decoration to provoke debate about their origins and connections. Researchers compared them with neighbouring and earlier traditions. Even an ordinary pot can raise a big historical question: who taught the potter to make it that way?

Sergiy Gorbanenko’s study of impressions at Bytytsia identified millet, barley, bread wheat, rye, emmer and oats, with rarer traces of other wheats. The marks preserve evidence of crops after the plants themselves decayed. A dent in clay can turn out to be a tiny record of farming.

The same study identified weed impressions as well as crops. Gorbanenko used them to argue for repeatedly cultivated ground and crops with different seasonal cycles. These are interpretations of botanical clues, rather than a surviving farming calendar, but they help reconstruct the work behind a household’s food supply.

sections.title: Later neighbours and what excavation corrected

items.text: Novotroitske, another site east of the imported outline, provides a ninth-century comparison after this card’s map interval. Lyapushkin excavated more than fifty partly sunken houses and about a hundred utility structures. These accumulated during the settlement’s occupation; the totals do not mean every building stood at once.

Older books imagined such settlements as networks of homes connected by covered passages. At Novotroitske, Lyapushkin found separate houses, even where they stood close together, and no connecting corridors. Careful excavation corrected an appealing picture that had been repeated as fact.

Ninth-century Novotroitske also yielded iron axes, adzes and spoon-carving tools, along with bone points and animal knucklebones bearing geometric marks. These objects offer glimpses of woodworking and small things people handled. The marked bones alone cannot tell us precisely who used them or whether a particular one was a toy.

sections.title: Tribute and a later written name

items.text: The Primary Chronicle says that Prince Oleh subdued the Severians in 884, imposed a light tribute and stopped their payments to the Khazars. This later account describes a change in political obligations. It belongs after the map’s eighth-century window.

In the Laurentian Chronicle manuscript of 1377, the account placed under 859 names them among people paying tribute. The National Library of Russia’s transcription has “на северех”, meaning “from the Severians” here. This is a later chronicle witness, not a contemporary eighth-century text written by the mapped communities.

ending.text: The map stops at 800, but Severian communities continued into the history of Rus’. The chronicle name is last reported in 1024, while related regional names survived much longer. The end of recorded use of a tribal name is not a date when its people disappeared.
